Evidence was gathered before a type was chosen. Outcome: no defensible discriminator; the subject meets open-case eligibility (adult, first professional role January 2024, first lead September 2026, record made of promotional cycles plus friendly testimony). Status ready, profile_format open_case, leading read Type 6 at low confidence, Type 9 as the alternative, Types 2 and 3 live; Types 1 and 4 considered and set aside. Risks set: contested_typing (required for open cases) and sensitive_allegations (a TMZ insinuation about her friendship with Sarah Paulson, C29, and an anonymous 2018 Page Six item about her Juilliard admission, C30), so the six-role jury applies.

Accuracy check (2026-10-18). Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story premiered on Netflix on September 17, 2026, and was No. 1 on the global English TV list in its first two weeks (14.5 million views for September 21-27, S23). Act One premiered at Tribeca on June 10, 2026; a 2027 theatrical release via Oscilloscope was reported by one outlet but not opened. The Bell Jar (Sarah Polley; she plays Joan) has wrapped and has no announced release date. Town & Country (September 23, 2026) mentions an unannounced project she was shooting in Los Angeles. No new casting announcement dated October 2026 was found. The most recent interview located (Wonderland, October 5, 2026) could not be opened. open_case.next_review is 2026-12-15, after the Golden Globe nominations expected in December.

Drafting guidance (open case). Follow the standard's 'Open case profiles' section. Open with who she is and why people are searching (her first lead, Netflix's No. 1 show, the famous parents), then name the open question: what her steady humility and her named fear are for. Show what the record shows, dated and sourced, with limits: the auditions (C05, C06), the way she meets the inheritance question (C07, C08), duty and preparation (C10-C13, C33), the trusted circle (C16, C17), the luck register (C14, C31), the worry and self-trust passage (C32), the discomfort with being public (C15), and the composure others see (C18, C19). Set Type 6 beside Types 9, 2 and 3 with the best evidence for and against each. Include an H2 beginning '## What would settle it' built from open_case.settle_signals. Keep '## What is Ella Beatty's personality type?' with an answer of at most 60 words in 'leading read, held loosely' language, for example: 'Leading read: Type 6, held loosely. Type 9 is the live alternative, with 2 and 3 still in play.' Target 1,200 to 2,500 words. Titles, description and FAQs must say 'leading read' or 'open case', never 'is a Type 6'. Set enneagram: 6 and published: false. The strongest hook candidates are verified and specific: she was waiting at the Carlyle before the Vogue reporter, following her father's 'Always be on time' (S01); she won Monster from a self-tape among seven (S19); in the same year she played a daughter dragged away from acting by her parents and a daughter who kills hers, and said 'What is the universe saying? I don't know... I'm going to be examining that' (S20).

Quotation cautions. (a) S03, S07, S08, S10 (broadcast captions), S13 video, S15, S16, S17, S18 and S19 are YouTube caption transcripts without speaker labels; check each printed quote against the audio and timestamp. (b) S05 is a Whisper transcript without speaker labels; quoted passages were re-transcribed with large-v3-turbo (see the S05 context), but confirm speaker by listening. In particular, the lines 'how do I be what you want... How do I be beautiful enough for you? How do I be interesting enough for you?' (about 35:56-36:06) may be the host's; do not attribute them to her without checking. (c) Variety's 'I've never played a true out-and-out villain' is Rebecca Hall's, not Beatty's (S12). (d) Charlie Hunnam's 'one of the best actresses he'll ever work with' is the Entertainment Tonight interviewer's report, not Hunnam on record (S08). (e) The TODAY captions render 'female rage and representation'; Netflix's statement gives 'female rage and repression'; quote neither from the captions. (f2) In S05 the line about legacy as 'that thing of feeling rooted in something and grounded in something that's such a gift' (about 45:38-45:59) and the rehearsal joke 'the worst actor ever' (about 09:15) cannot be assigned to a speaker from the transcript; do not attribute them to her without listening. (f) The Broadway.com write-up lines ('I am who I am', 'She's why I'm who I am', 'There's definitely a privilege...') were obtained through a summarizing fetch and are not in the 7-minute video; verify before quoting. (g) WWD quotes (Gus Van Sant, the Feud notebook) are secondhand via Biography.com (S22). (h) The New York Times review line 'fulfill[ed] the play's plan perfectly' is quoted from Town & Country (S20); open the review before quoting it directly. (i) In the ScreenRant roundtable (S19) use the original English caption track; the alternate track is a machine translation. Speakers there: Beatty to about 03:05, Hunnam to about 06:55, Max Winkler after. (j) Ian Brennan's 'blank slate' and 'innocence' quotes come from an unopened TV Insider piece (S28); do not use.

Sensitivity. Never repeat, link or allude to the TMZ insinuation about Beatty and Sarah Paulson (C29, S24); describe the friendship only in the two women's own words. Do not use the 2018 Page Six admissions item (C30, S25) unless the original is opened, and then only as an attributed, unconfirmed gossip report with the context that she auditioned and completed the four-year program. Do not name or characterize her siblings. Do not read Lizzie Borden, or Act One's parents, into her family (the queue note says so explicitly); her account of her parents is warm and is the only account on record. Do not speculate about her parents' ages or health. No diagnosis-like language about anxiety: 'nervous', 'scared' and 'worry' are her words; keep them hers.

Follow-ups worth doing before or at the next refresh: (1) open the Forbes Q&A (S26), the Wonderland interview (S27) and the TV Insider piece with Ian Brennan's casting quotes (S28) from a different network or through a subscription; (2) find and open the WWD 2024 and 2025 interviews, the full Broadway.com Show People episode and the New York Times review of Sexual Misconduct of the Middle Classes; (3) listen to S05 at 23:15-26:00, 29:55-32:00 and 33:50-37:40 to confirm speaker attribution; (4) look for any long-form interview or podcast given after September 2026, and for Golden Globe or other awards-season interviews; (5) search for testimony from Juilliard faculty or classmates, or from the Ghosts company (Billy Crudup, Lily Rabe, Jack O'Brien); (6) if the Page Six original surfaces, record exactly what it claims and who it cites.

Intro paragraph (Paulson and Esper chose her; 'I had no idea who your parents were'); offer 'the next morning'; Paulson: 'self-possessed'; surname exchange ('It really never occurred to me until I started working... responsibility towards an artistic legacy'); 'Always, always' and make-believe; 'Appropriate really changed my life'; pressure answer ('responsibility to honor what the other actors are doing... sources.excerpt: “The pressure that I felt had to do with the responsibility to honor what the other actors are doing. You don’t want to leave people in the lurch. You want to show up and support people [...] I also felt like, ‘Okay, they’ve given me this job, so I better show up.’ I didn’t have a lot of time to be scared” [...] “I think her inability to not tell the truth is something I relate to. I am not a good liar. I have a hard time not being totally earnest.” [...] “Sometimes we have four or five days between performances and I get really nervous.”
sources.context: Long conversation recorded on Zoom in May 2025 during the Sexual Misconduct of the Middle Classes run. The interviewer is her close friend and former co-star, so this is both self-report and friendly testimony (Paulson: 'The thing that comes to mind most clearly is self-possessed'). The register is affectionate and joking ('my Venmo is...', astrology), which should be read as banter.

sources.excerpt: “And being present and kind of being where your feet are, it's something I try to try really hard and fail at often frequently to live by. It's just like, you know, so much of what we worry about in life, so many of the things that we are so, so emotionally fraught about, you know, you can't handle until you're there. And I think trusting yourself to have, you know, the tools and the ability to handle it when you're faced with it is something I'm still really trying to do. And God knows that was something I did in that play.” [...] “I think because I felt that assurance from her going into it, I didn't feel a pressure to replicate anybody else's [...] you can't just come in and do whatever you want, but you serve the play” [...] “there's a part of me that feels like, Oh my God, I can't believe they picked me”
sources.context: The longest first-person source: a relaxed 52-minute conversation with Anthony Meindl, an acting teacher who calls her 'my dear friend', recorded early in 2025 while she was rehearsing Ghosts. The host talks at length and steers toward his podcast's theme of presence, so some of her statements extend his points. No speaker labels: the episode was transcribed locally with Whisper small.en, and the quoted passages were re-transcribed with large-v3-turbo; wording differences between the two runs are minor (for example 'helped' vs 'held me and supported me'; 'serve the plate' is Whisper's mishearing of 'serve the play'). Speaker attribution follows the conversational turns and should be confirmed by listening, especially around 35:56-36:06, where lines about trying to 'be what you want' may be the host's. Draft stage: quotations restore a mid-sentence 'um' where spoken and drop leading 'and, uh' and repeated false starts only at the start of a quotation; checked against the large-v3-turbo clips (clip_a, clip_b, clip_c, clip_h).

claims.claim: Vogue's reporter arrived at 2:58 p.m. for a 3 p.m. meeting at the Carlyle, a Manhattan hotel, in February 2024 and found Beatty already there with her coat folded over her arm; Beatty was following her father Warren Beatty's rule 'Always be on time' ('Or, in her case, early').
claims.passage: Vogue's Elise Taylor arrived at the Manhattan hotel at 2:58 p.m. for a 3 p.m. coffee in February 2024, expecting to wait. Beatty was already there, her coat neatly folded over her arm, following one of her father Warren Beatty's cardinal rules: "Always be on time." In her case, early.
claims.inference: One observed instance, reported by the writer (S01). It shows reliability and pre-emptive care about expectations in a first major interview; the rule is her report of her father's advice.
claims.alternative: Punctuality for a Vogue interview is ordinary professionalism and a single occasion. 'In her case, early' paraphrases Taylor's own aside. The 'Be kind' and 'listen' rules from the same article are not used in the draft except 'listen' via TODAY (C56).

claims.claim: In February 2024 she raised the nepotism question before the Vogue reporter asked it ('without me even asking', per Taylor) and answered: 'I totally acknowledge that there is an inherent privilege and exposure that comes from having well-known actors as parents... And I really hope that I can offer something meaningful.'
claims.passage: Then, before Taylor could ask, Beatty raised the subject every story about her would raise. "I totally acknowledge that there is an inherent privilege and exposure that comes from having well-known actors as parents," she told [Vogue](https://www.vogue.com/article/meet-ella-beatty-the-breakout-star-of-feud-whos-now-heading-to-broadway). "And I really hope that I can offer something meaningful."
claims.inference: The unprompted move is the reporter's observation (S01); the wording is hers and is stable from 2024 to 2025 (S01, S04; a near-identical line in the Broadway.com write-up of S03 is unverified). She names the advantage, does not argue with it, and promises work in return. That pre-emptive acknowledgment of a likely criticism fits Six (anticipating the objection), One (owning what is fair) and Three (managing the image) about equally.
claims.alternative: This is also the answer any publicist would recommend to a famous child debuting after the 'nepo baby' backlash (Vogue itself calls it 'the nepo-baby discourse'). On its own it shows media competence, not motive.

claims.claim: Vogue's Elise Taylor described her as 'Exceptionally poised' (February 2024).
claims.passage: Taylor's words for her were "Exceptionally poised."
claims.inference: A reporter's observation in a promotional interview; it is the first instance of the composure others repeatedly describe (see C18).
claims.alternative: One writer's impression over tea; poise in interviews can be trained and is expected of a famous child.

claims.claim: Sarah Paulson, who starred opposite her in Appropriate on Broadway, told Town & Country in September 2026: 'There is something unnervingly, dazzlingly self-assured about Ella.'
claims.passage: Sarah Paulson, who starred opposite her on Broadway in _Appropriate_, told [Town & Country](https://www.townandcountrymag.com/leisure/arts-and-culture/a73571951/ella-beatty-lizzie-borden-interview-2026/) in September 2026, "There is something unnervingly, dazzlingly self-assured about Ella."
claims.inference: The gap between outer composure and inner report is the most interesting unexplained feature of the record. Composure over private nerves fits a Six who has prepared, a Nine whose calm surface hides inner activity, and a Three whose presentation is polished.
claims.alternative: Paulson is an interested witness: in Interview (S04) she calls Beatty 'a person I'm wildly close to', and Beatty calls her 'one of my very best friends in the world' (TODAY, S10). A friend's flattering description in a cover story is not neutral. The draft's author-voice label 'now one of her closest friends' was replaced by a stable fact (co-star) so that no relationship status sits in the author's voice.
claims.review_trigger: Recheck if either woman describes the relationship differently on record; describe it only in their own words, and never allude to S24.

claims.claim: She told Variety (September 17, 2026) that she made the audition tape thinking 'I understand this person', and that 'When I found out that I had gotten the part, I was over the moon and also really scared.'
claims.passage: Beatty describes both. She told [Variety](https://variety.com/2026/tv/features/monster-lizzie-borden-ella-beatty-1236866041/) that month that she made her audition tape thinking, "I understand this person." Then: "When I found out that I had gotten the part, I was over the moon and also really scared."
claims.inference: Her account holds confidence and fear together: she felt she understood the character, then felt 'over the moon and also really scared'. The fear half supports the Six read; the confidence half is why the paragraph says 'both' rather than setting her account against Paulson's.
claims.alternative: Nervous excitement is ordinary for a first lead. Entertainment Tonight has the same confidence ('I felt like I kind of got her', S08), and No Intervals tells the landing-the-role story with excitement and luck and no fear at all (S16).

claims.inference: Year, birthplace, birth order and parents are consistent across Wikipedia (S21), Biography.com (S22) and Town & Country ('The youngest of four siblings', S20). Town & Country reports plays 'at summer camp and community theater' (Snoopy, Sandy in Annie); she told Broadway.com in 2024 she did 'so much theater' as a kid (S03).

claims.passage: She trained at Juilliard from 2018 to 2022 and, as she told Paulson, "didn't work professionally at all until I graduated from acting school."
claims.inference: Childhood roles and camp are her own account (S03, about 01:46-03:09) and Town & Country's (S20). Juilliard entry in 2018 is from Vogue (S01); graduation in 2022 from Deadline (S09), Biography.com (S22) and Town & Country ('just two years out of Juilliard' in 2024, S20). 'I didn't work professionally at all until I graduated from acting school' is hers (S04). Town & Country adds that the pandemic moved part of her training to Zoom. In February 2025 she said: 'I was 18 when I went to Juilliard and I didn't have any kind of a professional career till I was like 22. So my childhood was really just play' (S05, about 40:58-41:11).
claims.alternative: Vogue's February 2024 phrase 'Now a year out of school' (S01) loosely conflicts with 2022; prefer 2022. Whether skipping child acting was her choice or her parents' rule is not on record; do not present it as her decision.

claims.claim: Her credits since January 2024: Feud: Capote vs. The Swans (FX, January 2024); replacing Elle Fanning in Appropriate on Broadway (2024); in 2025 her film debut in If I Had Legs I'd Kick You (Sundance), Ibsen's Ghosts at Lincoln Center Theater, and Sexual Misconduct of the Middle Classes, a two-hander opposite Hugh Jackman; the lead in Sophia Takal's Act One, which premiered at Tribeca in June 2026.
claims.passage: Since January 2024 she has gone from FX's _Feud: Capote vs. The Swans_ to Broadway, replacing Elle Fanning in _Appropriate_; to her 2025 film debut in _If I Had Legs I'd Kick You_, Ibsen's _Ghosts_ at Lincoln Center Theater and _Sexual Misconduct of the Middle Classes_, a two-hander opposite [Hugh Jackman](/personality-analysis/hugh-jackman); and to the lead in _Act One_, which premiered at Tribeca in June 2026.
claims.inference: The sequence is consistent across Wikipedia (S21: If I Had Legs 2025 film debut, Ghosts 2025 at Lincoln Center), Town & Country (S20: 'If I Had Legs I'd Kick You', 'a Lincoln Center Theater production of Henrik Ibsen's Ghosts', Act One 'premiered... at this past spring's Tribeca'), Interview (S04: Sexual Misconduct is 'a juicy two-hander'), IndieWire on Act One (S06, June 9, 2026) and Deadline (S09). Her first professional screen work aired in January 2024; her first film lead (Act One) premiered in June 2026 and her first series lead (Monster) in September 2026.
claims.alternative: Release plans for Act One (a 2027 theatrical release via Oscilloscope was reported by one outlet, not opened) and The Bell Jar are unconfirmed. Town & Country (S20) mentions an unannounced project she was shooting in Los Angeles in September 2026.
claims.review_trigger: Update when The Bell Jar or Act One receives a release date or is released, or when a new lead role is announced.

claims.claim: Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story, the fourth season of Ryan Murphy and Ian Brennan's Netflix anthology, premiered on September 17, 2026, with Beatty in the title role.
claims.passage: _Monster_, Ryan Murphy and Ian Brennan's Netflix anthology, premiered on September 17, 2026.
claims.inference: Netflix's Tudum feature and Variety's junket piece were published on premiere day; Tudum names Murphy and Brennan as the anthology's creators.
claims.alternative: None material; the premiere date is a matter of record.

claims.claim: Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story was No. 1 on Netflix's global English-language TV list in its first two weeks, with 14.5 million views in its second week (September 21-27, 2026), up 20% from its first.
claims.passage: In its second week it drew 14.5 million views and topped Netflix's global English-language TV list, [TheWrap](https://www.thewrap.com/creative-content/tv-shows/monster-the-lizzie-borden-story-ratings-viewership-week-2-netflix/) reported.
claims.inference: TheWrap's report of Netflix's own Top 10 data (S23). It explains why search interest in her spiked in late September 2026.
claims.alternative: Netflix-reported views are not independently audited. Early critics' scores for the season were mixed (reported, not opened); praise for her performance in individual reviews was not opened and should not be summarized.
claims.review_trigger: Recheck if Netflix announces a renewal, total viewing figures, or awards nominations (for example the Golden Globes).

claims.claim: She appears in Sarah Polley's film adaptation of The Bell Jar opposite Billie Eilish (and Carey Mulligan); no release date had been announced as of October 18, 2026.
claims.passage: She also appears in Sarah Polley's film of _The Bell Jar_, opposite [Billie Eilish](/personality-analysis/billie-eilish), which had no release date as of October 18, 2026.
claims.inference: Town & Country (September 2026) reports she is 'set to appear opposite Billie Eilish and Carey Mulligan in a film adaptation of Sylvia Plath's The Bell Jar directed by Sarah Polley'; Wikipedia lists the film in post-production. The research stage's 'Joan' role was not found in the saved sources and was dropped.

claims.claim: Since the September 2026 premiere people have been searching for her; her public record begins in January 2024, is mostly promotional, and holds a gap between the composure colleagues describe and the fear she names beside excitement.
claims.passage: Since the premiere, people have been looking her up. They find a mostly promotional record that begins in January 2024, with a gap running through it: colleagues describe composure, while she names fear beside the excitement. This is an open case: a leading read held loosely, the alternatives beside it, and what would decide between them.
claims.inference: The record runs from the January 2024 Feud debut and the February 2024 Vogue profile (S01) to late September 2026 (S19, S20). Composure: 'Exceptionally poised' (S01), 'self-assured' (S20), 'self-possessed' (S04), 'fearless' (S20). Fear beside excitement: 'over the moon and also really scared' (S12), 'I was so excited... And then I also felt, How am I gonna do this' (S14).
claims.alternative: The same gap is ordinary for a young actor in a first lead under nepotism scrutiny; it may describe circumstance rather than motive. The relative phrase "under three years old" was replaced with absolute dates (future-01).
claims.review_trigger: Reopen at open_case.next_review (2026-12-15) or when a long-form interview or third-party testimony from before 2024 appears.

claims.claim: Leading read Type 6 at low confidence; Type 9 is the main alternative; Types 2 and 3 remain live. She talks about responsibility (to castmates, her family legacy, the real Lizzie Borden) and meets it with preparation (showing up off book). Her public record starts in 2024.
claims.passage: Leading read: Enneagram Type 6, held loosely at low confidence. Type 9 is the main alternative; Types 2 and 3 remain in play. She talks about responsibility (to her castmates, her family's legacy, the real Lizzie Borden) and meets it by showing up off book. Her public record starts in 2024, so nothing yet separates these reads.
claims.inference: Mirrors type_hypothesis and open_case. Responsibility to castmates: 'The pressure that I felt had to do with the responsibility to honor what the other actors are doing' (S04). Family legacy: 'a kind of responsibility towards an artistic legacy' (S04). The real person: 'a huge responsibility to the part, to the anthology, to the real person' (S12). Off book: S05 ('came in off book') and S20 ('show up off-book'). Record start: Feud, January 2024 (S01, S21). Appears in the body and verbatim as the first FAQ answer.
claims.alternative: See type_hypothesis.against: colleagues describe composure, some preparation is framed as excitement, and nothing shows her in conflict. 'Responsibility' is also a One and Two word.
claims.review_trigger: Revise when any open_case.settle_signals event occurs or at the 2026-12-15 review.

claims.claim: Of the triad emotions (fear, anger, shame), fear is the one she names outright, usually when asked about pressure and usually beside excitement or luck; that is why Six leads, but fear is also expected of an actor in a first lead.
claims.passage: Of those three emotions, fear is the one she names outright, usually when asked about pressure and usually beside excitement or luck. That is why Six leads, and why it can't lead by much: fear is also the ordinary weather of an actor in her first lead.
claims.inference: Fear statements: 'over the moon and also really scared' (S12), 'I was so excited... And then I also felt, How am I gonna do this' (S14), 'I get really nervous' (S04), auditions 'such a vulnerable, scary thing' (S05), the Appropriate takeover 'felt new and scary and challenging' (S05 clip_b). No statement of her own anger or shame was found; 'self-conscious' appears only as something she had no time for (S05). The narrower wording replaces the draft's 'the emotion Beatty names most', which the subject and Enneagram reviewers showed is false as a frequency claim: luck and excitement words outnumber fear words in the saved transcripts ('the luckiest lady in the world', S08; 'I was really excited. I felt very lucky', S16).
claims.alternative: Self-report in promotional settings; a Nine, Three or Seven could report first-lead nerves too. Her commonest register (excitement, luck, curiosity) is the case for Type 7, which the weighing section tests and sets aside.

claims.claim: Asked by Paulson (Interview, recorded May 2025, published June 5, 2025) whether at Juilliard she ever thought she shouldn't use her last name, she said no and: 'It really never occurred to me until I started working. I do feel a kind of responsibility towards an artistic legacy that I don't feel ashamed of... I'd hope that my work would be enough to make me separate, but I also understand why people do that.'
claims.passage: "It really never occurred to me until I started working. I do feel a kind of responsibility towards an artistic legacy that I don't feel ashamed of... I'd hope that my work would be enough to make me separate, but I also understand why people do that."
claims.inference: Her answer pairs responsibility to a family legacy with the hope of being judged on her work; it repeats the 2024 Vogue shape (C07).
claims.alternative: Interviewer is her close friend; the answer is also standard media practice for a famous child.

claims.claim: Her handling of the inheritance question is consistent from 2024 to 2025 (name the advantage, don't argue, promise work); it is also the answer any famous child would be advised to give after the 'nepo baby' backlash, so on its own it cannot show motive.
claims.passage: The answer hasn't changed shape since Vogue: name the advantage, don't argue with it, promise work in return. It is also the answer any famous child would be advised to give after the "nepo baby" backlash, so on its own it cannot show motive.
claims.inference: Same structure in S01 (February 2024) and S04 (May 2025). The sentence states the media-practice alternative without ruling on it and implies no coaching; the draft's undated-but-wrong '2024 "nepo baby" moment' and 'shows media sense more than motive' were removed (fan-07, subject-F7).
claims.alternative: Could reflect sincere conviction; the record cannot separate the two.

claims.claim: For Appropriate, Paulson and Michael Esper read with several actresses; Paulson recalls 'when you walked out, Michael and I turned to each other and we're like, "It's got to be Ella Beatty"' and told her 'I had no idea who your parents were.' Paulson is an interested witness who, in the same conversation, calls Beatty 'a person I'm wildly close to.'
claims.passage: The casting stories come from people who are not neutral. For _Appropriate_, Paulson and her co-star Michael Esper read with several actresses. "When you walked out, Michael and I turned to each other and we're like, 'It's got to be Ella Beatty,'" Paulson recalled in that conversation, in which she calls Beatty "a person I'm wildly close to." She also told her, "I had no idea who your parents were."
claims.inference: Paulson's account in Interview (S04) and Town & Country (S20). A casting by audition, with a lead actor claiming no knowledge of her parents. The paragraph now presents the casting stories as testimony from interested people rather than as verification (critic-08).
claims.alternative: Paulson is a close friend and a Monster co-star, so her testimony is affectionate and interested. In the same answer she hedges: 'If your last name were Bening, it might be a little bit different' (S04).

claims.claim: Max Winkler (director of six of eight episodes, executive producer) told ScreenRant that after watching a self-tape from casting director Tiffany Little Canfield he called Ryan Murphy and said 'We got her'; Murphy watched the seven tapes without being told which one and asked 'Is it Ella?'. She had worked with Murphy on Feud.
claims.passage: _Monster_ came from a self-tape. Max Winkler, who directed six of the eight episodes, told [ScreenRant](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RooR7nJOmiM) that after watching a tape from casting director Tiffany Little Canfield he called Murphy and said, "We got her." Murphy watched all seven tapes without being told which one, then called back and asked, "Is it Ella?" Both men are selling the show, and she had already worked for Murphy on _Feud_, so no one can measure what the name did before the tape. The accounts agree that a tape was required.
claims.inference: Winkler's account (S19, audio re-checked) agrees with Town & Country's report of a self-taped audition (S20); Deadline reported an 'extensive multi-country casting search' (S09). The record shows a tape was required; it cannot measure what the name did before it.
claims.alternative: Winkler and Murphy are interested parties promoting the show, Winkler is himself the son of a famous actor (S20), and a prior working relationship with Murphy plus her name can open the door to an audition. The record cannot measure how much the name helped, only that a tape was required.

claims.claim: She told Variety she felt 'a huge responsibility to the part, to the anthology, to the real person' on getting the Monster role.
claims.passage: "I felt a huge responsibility to the part, to the anthology, to the real person," she told Variety.
claims.inference: Part of the same Variety answer as C11; the obligation runs to the work and to people, alongside fear.
claims.alternative: 'Honoring the real person' is stock junket language for a biographical role.

claims.claim: At the September 9, 2026 Netflix press conference (Showbiz Junkies report) she said: 'I was so excited. I was over the moon. And then I also felt, "How am I gonna do this and what does it mean?"' and that starting work before pre-production helped because 'all of those things that aren't necessarily tangible work can help you feel like you're starting.'
claims.passage: At Netflix's September 9 press conference, [reported by Showbiz Junkies](https://www.showbizjunkies.com/tv/netflix-monster-lizzie-borden-cast-press-conference/), she said, "I was so excited. I was over the moon. And then I also felt, 'How am I gonna do this and what does it mean?'" So she started before pre-production, because that work "can help you feel like you're starting."
claims.inference: Fear named beside excitement, then answered by starting work early. That sequence (anxiety met by securing the ground) is the behavior the Six read rests on. The draft's claim that the same-room contrast with Rebecca Hall shows this was her choice rather than the role's demand was withdrawn: Hall gave an artistic reason, all three actors converged on the script, and Beatty had the title role (fan-01, critic-01, enneagram-05, subject-F3, unfamiliar-01).
claims.alternative: First-lead nerves are universal; early work on a title role about a real, heavily documented person is ordinary. A Three would also prepare hard for a career-making role, and a One would research to get it right. All accounts are hers.

claims.claim: She told Collider: 'Right away, when I found out I had the part, I listened to every single podcast and video that's ever been published in the world. I couldn't be stopped if I had a WiFi connection. But I started to hone in and get a little bit more specific, and I did feel that my responsibility was to what was on the page.'
claims.passage: She told [Collider](https://collider.com/monster-lizzie-borden-story-netflix-ella-beatty/) that she "listened to every single podcast and video that's ever been published in the world. I couldn't be stopped if I had a WiFi connection." Then she narrowed to "what was on the page."
claims.inference: Heavy research followed by narrowing to the script (critic-03 asked for the narrowing to be shown). No Intervals tells the same research as excitement: 'I was so excited to immediately just delve into every podcast' (S16), which the Six 'against' paragraph now quotes.
claims.alternative: Heavy research for a historical title role is common.

claims.claim: She told her friend Anthony Meindl (In The Moment, February 2025) that before replacing Elle Fanning in Appropriate she had about two days of table work, learned the blocking from a video and the understudies, and 'came in off book, so that would never be an issue', then opened after a Tuesday-to-Friday tech at the Belasco; director Lila Neugebauer told her from the start to find her own version, and 'because I felt that assurance from her going into it, I didn't feel a pressure to replicate anybody else's.'
claims.passage: _Appropriate_ was the same move under more pressure. She told her friend the acting teacher Anthony Meindl, on his [_In The Moment_ podcast](https://soundcloud.com/anthonymeindl/anthonyinterviewsellabeatty) in February 2025, that she had about two days of table work before taking over, learned the blocking from a video and the understudies, and "came in off book, so that would never be an issue." She opened after a few days of tech at the Belasco Theatre. The director, Lila Neugebauer, told her from the start to find her own version. "Because I felt that assurance from her going into it, I didn't feel a pressure to replicate anybody else's," Beatty said.
claims.inference: A concrete episode told twice (S05 at length; S04: 'We rehearsed when we teched at the Belasco... I had to learn on the job'). Meindl opens the episode with 'my dear friend Ella Beatty' (S05, about 01:00). The sequence is: remove the controllable risk (lines), take permission from the authority in charge, then contribute. That ordering is Six-like; serving the structure is also Nine-like and One-like.
claims.alternative: Learning lines before a put-in is basic professionalism, and directors routinely tell replacements not to imitate. The apology joke is self-deprecating banter. Her account only.

claims.claim: The Appropriate sequence runs: remove the controllable risk, take permission from the authority in charge, then contribute.
claims.passage: First she removed the risk she could control. Then she took permission from the person in charge. Then she brought herself.
claims.inference: Ordering drawn from her own account (C33). Securing ground before contributing is Six-like.
claims.alternative: Serving the existing structure also fits Nine and One; learning lines first is basic professionalism.

claims.claim: During the 2025 run of Sexual Misconduct of the Middle Classes she said she missed the play on nights off, 'Sometimes we have four or five days between performances and I get really nervous,' and took home director Ian Rickson's 'diary book' of rehearsal images and writings.
claims.passage: On nights off from _Sexual Misconduct of the Middle Classes_ in 2025, she missed the play. "Sometimes we have four or five days between performances and I get really nervous," she told Paulson, so she took home the director's "diary book" from rehearsals.
claims.inference: The nerves are tied to time away from the play; her remedy is a trusted reference object from the director. Anxiety answered by structure.
claims.alternative: Her stated reason is missing the characters, not fear of failure; the diary book was the director's own creation, so using it reflects his culture as well as her temperament.

claims.claim: She told Town & Country her method as a newcomer: 'I felt the best thing to do was to sit very quietly, watch, and pray, and then work extremely hard and show up off-book.'
claims.passage: Her approach as a newcomer, she told Town & Country, was to "sit very quietly, watch, and pray, and then work extremely hard and show up off-book."
claims.inference: Her own account in 2024 and 2026, corroborated by Jackman's testimony in Town & Country (S20). Preparation and observation are how she manages being new among famous people.
claims.alternative: Conservatory training and ordinary replacement-actor diligence explain much of this, and a famous name raises the cost of being caught unprepared. Jackman co-starred and the production was his company's, so he is an interested party. 'Pray' is a figure of speech, not a religious claim.

claims.claim: Asked by Paulson what pressure she felt coming into Appropriate, she said: 'The pressure that I felt had to do with the responsibility to honor what the other actors are doing. You don't want to leave people in the lurch.' Later in the same answer: 'I didn't have a lot of time to be scared because I got the job and then we started.' Hugh Jackman told Town & Country she is 'always prepared, kind, funny, and fearless'; Paulson's first impression was 'self-possessed'.
claims.passage: The record pushes back too. Asked by Paulson what pressure she had felt coming into _Appropriate_, she named other people before fear: "The pressure that I felt had to do with the responsibility to honor what the other actors are doing. You don't want to leave people in the lurch." Later in the same answer: "I didn't have a lot of time to be scared because I got the job and then we started." The people who work with her see composure. Jackman told Town & Country she is "always prepared, kind, funny, and fearless." Paulson's word is "self-possessed."
claims.inference: Her one direct answer about what pressure means names obligation to the group before fear (enneagram-03, fan-02, critic-02). The no-time-to-be-scared half and colleagues' composure weaken a fear-first Six; the obligation half is the Six case's most type-specific strand (duty and loyalty to the company) and is also live Two evidence ('support people').
claims.alternative: Jackman and Paulson are collaborators and friends promoting shared work; composure over private nerves is also compatible with Six.

claims.claim: Speaking to Meindl during Ghosts rehearsals (February 2025), she said of the Appropriate takeover: 'part of what was so great about it is that I didn't have time to worry about it... I didn't really have time to get self-conscious or, um, you know, self-involved about it', and that she had 'so many things to serve and so many people to please.'
claims.passage: Talking to Meindl during _Ghosts_ rehearsals, she found an upside in the rush of the _Appropriate_ takeover. "Part of what was so great about it is that I didn't have time to worry about it," she said. "I didn't really have time to get self-conscious or, um, you know, self-involved about it." She had "so many things to serve and so many people to please."
claims.inference: She experiences being too busy to worry as relief, and the same sentence names an outward load (things to serve, people to please). The restored clause comes from the large-v3-turbo re-transcription (clip_b: 'i had so much to do and so many things to serve and so many people to please'); the article quotes only the words both Whisper passes agree on. Speaker: a female voice by the subject and critic reviewers' pitch checks; the host's turns are separate.
claims.alternative: Whisper transcript, no speaker labels; attribution follows the turn (the host asks about the role, she answers) and the reviewers' pitch analysis, not a human listen.

claims.claim: She described worry as a habit she works against: 'Being present and kind of being where your feet are, it's something I try to try really hard and fail at often frequently to live by... trusting yourself to have, you know, the tools and the ability to handle it when you're faced with it is, um, something I'm still really trying to do. And God knows that was something I did in that play' (of Appropriate, February 2025).
claims.passage: "Being present and kind of being where your feet are, it's something I try to try really hard and fail at often frequently to live by. It's just like, you know, so much of what we worry about in life, so many of the things that we are so, so emotionally fraught about, you know, you can't handle until you're there. And I think trusting yourself to have, you know, the tools and the ability to handle it when you're faced with it is, um, something I'm still really trying to do. And God knows that was something I did in that play."
claims.inference: This is the most specific self-description in the record and the strongest single support for the Six reading: anticipatory worry plus a stated, ongoing effort to trust her own capacity to cope. That is the Six's characteristic growth task. The speed-round lines repeat the theme in a joking register. It is unprompted in the sense that she extends the host's point about tragedy into a statement about herself.
claims.alternative: A single interview with a friend and acting teacher whose theme that day was presence ('In the Moment'); she may be echoing the host's framing. Nine also strives to be 'where your feet are' and could describe the same struggle as getting lost in others' agendas rather than in worry. The speed-round 'Everything. Ghosts.' is a joke riffing on the episode's ghosts theme. Auto-transcribed with Whisper; no speaker labels; attribution follows the conversational turn ('that play' is Appropriate, her show, not the host's). The draft quotes it with 'um' restored and the opening 'and, uh' dropped; the line follows the host's monologue about wasted worry, and 'that play' (Appropriate) and the host's reply 'I'm sorry I missed it' confirm the speaker.

claims.claim: The worry/self-trust passage supports Six (growth task of trusting one's capacity to cope), Nine (relief at having no room for self) and Two ('so many people to please').
claims.passage: Read as a Six, that is the type's growth task in her own words: learning to trust that she can handle what she fears before it arrives. Read as a Nine, the telling detail comes first. The rush felt good because it left no room for her. Read as a Two, the clause that matters sits in between: "so many people to please."
claims.inference: All parts of the same answer (C51, C32) are set side by side so no live reading gets only the friendly half.
claims.alternative: May echo the host's theme of presence; a single conversation with a friend.

claims.claim: In 2026 she told Town & Country she has 'a certain amount of discomfort about being a public person' and wants 'to be able to disappear into roles', while 'There is also joy in sharing your life with people.' These, with her credit to luck and others, are the Nine case.
claims.passage: The Nine case is how she presents: credit to luck and others, "a certain amount of discomfort about being a public person" and a wish "to be able to disappear into roles," as she told Town & Country in 2026. She added, "There is also joy in sharing your life with people."
claims.inference: Supports Nine (self-forgetting) or Six (visibility as exposure); counts against an image-first Three. The draft's Paulson line 'It's a relief to come to work and remember you're being someone else' was removed from the Nine case: in Interview (S04) she said it of the role she called 'the closest to me', about keeping a boundary with a character, not a wish to vanish (critic-04, subject-F6). The Town & Country 'disappear into roles' line supports the Nine point directly.
claims.alternative: She allows that this may 'change and fluctuate with time', so it is a current position. Reticence can be strategy for an actor whose name already draws attention; she keeps a public Instagram account and does extensive press.
claims.review_trigger: Recheck after her next major press cycle (for example The Bell Jar release or awards season): has her stated comfort with public life changed?

claims.claim: She credits luck: 'I feel like the luckiest lady in the world' (Entertainment Tonight, September 12, 2026, audio re-checked); the same register appears on TODAY ('I can't believe my luck'), at Tribeca and in the 2025 podcast.
claims.passage: Credit runs the same way. "I feel like the luckiest lady in the world," she told [Entertainment Tonight](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DdDLa9vctOA) before the premiere.
claims.inference: The pattern appears in every 2026 interview, including unscripted carpet and morning-show settings, and she volunteers the deflection herself (S20). It argues against an image-first Three reading, which would more often own the result, and fits Nine (self-minimizing), Six (credit to the group and its leaders) and Two (attention on others). The 2025 podcast repeats the register outside a junket: 'I was so lucky. And I was so lucky' (S05, about 24:05-24:13), 'So I'm so lucky. I'm so lucky' (about 47:05).
claims.alternative: This is the expected register for a famous child in nepotism-conscious press and for any newcomer on a junket; publicists coach it. Effusive praise of co-stars ('She's the best', S13) is junket convention. The pattern shows how she presents, not necessarily what she believes.

claims.claim: She told Meindl (February 2025) that she still feels disbelief 'about every project that I've ever done... there's a part of me that feels like, Oh my God, I can't believe they picked me.'
claims.passage: Of every project she has done, she told Meindl, "there's a part of me that feels like, Oh my God, I can't believe they picked me."
claims.inference: Consistent across an unhurried 52-minute conversation with a friend (S05, about 09:58-10:11 and 34:28-34:47) and a 2026 junket (S08). The expectation of rejection is a habit of mind she describes, not only a polite phrase. It fits Six (anticipating the bad outcome) and Nine (self-discounting) and argues against an achievement-confident Three.
claims.alternative: Surprise at being cast is universal among young actors and is the humble answer a famous child is expected to give. 'Every project' includes jobs she got after auditioning against many others, which makes the surprise plausible as sincere.

claims.claim: Asked by Town & Country how she had changed, she said, 'I'll answer authentically even though I want to deflect.'
claims.passage: Asked by Town & Country how she had changed, she flagged the reflex first: "I'll answer authentically even though I want to deflect."
claims.inference: She names her own deflection reflex, which argues against an image-first Three reading.
claims.alternative: Said 'with a laugh'; a light framing of an ordinary interview move.

claims.claim: Her credit-deflection fits Nine's self-discounting or Six's expectation of the worse outcome better than a Three's ownership of results.
claims.passage: That fits a Nine's self-discounting or a Six's expectation of the worse outcome better than a Three's ownership of results.
claims.inference: Draws on C14, C31 and C53.
claims.alternative: Publicists coach this register; it shows presentation, not necessarily belief. The Three section states that these press statements cannot by themselves rule Three out (enneagram-08).

claims.claim: She keeps a small, close circle: asked on TODAY (September 2026) how Paulson supports her, 'We call every 15 minutes' and Paulson is 'there for advice at any minute'; with her mother it's 'once a day, debrief', and her mother is 'big on not giving you the answer' (Drew Barrymore, September 2026).
claims.passage: She keeps a small, close circle. Asked on [TODAY](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Q6n83ZQZX2w) in September 2026 how Paulson supports her, she said, "We call every 15 minutes," and that Paulson is "there for advice at any minute." With her mother it's "once a day, debrief," she told [Drew Barrymore](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=GYkLldtGQ3s), adding that her mother is "big on not giving you the answer."

type_hypothesis.against: (1) The people who work with her describe composure, not anxiety: Sarah Paulson's 'self-possessed' and 'unnervingly, dazzlingly self-assured' (C18, C50), Hugh Jackman's 'fearless' (C50), Max Winkler's 'wide-eyedness' (C19). (2) There is no sign of the questioning or testing of authority that usually accompanies Six; she attaches fast ('She's one of my very best friends in the world... we just kind of fell in love immediately', C13). (3) Town & Country's Naveen Kumar sees 'a thoughtful relationship to uncertainty' that she 'seems to be comfortable with—and maybe even covets in her work' (C82), which sits awkwardly with a Six's search for solid ground. (4) Some preparation she frames as excitement, not fear ('I was so excited to immediately just delve into every podcast', S16); fear is the triad emotion she names, but excitement, luck and curiosity are her commonest register (C42). (5) Every worry statement is self-report, the two longest conversations are with friends (Paulson, S04; Anthony Meindl, S05), and first-lead nerves, audition dread and heavy preparation are ordinary for any young actor. (6) Nepotism scrutiny supplies a non-type reason for her humility, preparation and pre-emptive acknowledgment of privilege (C07, C43). type_hypothesis.alternative_case: Type 9 explains much of how she presents: credit goes to luck and to others (C14, C31, C53); she has 'a certain amount of discomfort about being a public person' and wants 'to be able to disappear into roles' (C15); she merges warmly with collaborators (C13, C19); the Appropriate rush felt good because it left no room for self-concern (C51, C52); and Kumar's observation that she is comfortable with uncertainty fits a Nine's ease (C82). Under pressure a Nine can take on Six-like worry and preparation, so the fear-then-preparation pattern does not exclude Nine (C61). What strains the Nine reading: she names fear and goes straight to work on it ('I think immediately I just wanted to start working on it', C60); her ambition is old and plain ('Always, always', C24); she gets 'really nervous' on nights off with nothing at stake (C49); and the core of the Nine case, how she handles her own anger, has no account on record (C83). Type 2 is live: fast attachments, praise for collaborators, 'my job as the actress was to love and advocate for the person' (S15), and accounts of pressure that point outward ('so many people to please', S05; 'You don't want to leave people in the lurch', S04) (C35, C50, C51); against it, no account shows care she gives unasked or resentment when it goes unnoticed, and she is mostly the one looked after. Type 3 is live: an unusually fast start (C03), polish ('Exceptionally poised', C37), unprompted management of the nepotism question (C07), and the hope that her work will 'make me separate' (C08); against it, the deflection she names (C53) and her discomfort with being public (C15), though these are press statements an image-adaptive Three could also give (C25), and no choice on record shows her taking a role for its size. Types 1, 4 and 7 were tested and set aside (C20): One fits her earnestness but nothing shows an inner critic aimed at standards; Four fits her sensitivity but she does not present herself as set apart; Seven fits her excitement, luck and curiosity, but she volunteers the painful feelings a Seven tends to steer around.
type_hypothesis.discriminator: None that is defensible yet. The best candidate strand for Six is what she says pressure is: responsibility to a group and to an inheritance ('The pressure that I felt had to do with the responsibility to honor what the other actors are doing. You don't want to leave people in the lurch', S04; 'a kind of responsibility towards an artistic legacy', S04; 'a huge responsibility to the part, to the anthology, to the real person', S12; 'my responsibility was to what was on the page', S13), met by securing the ground before she brings herself (off book 'so that would never be an issue', S05; starting before pre-production, S14; the director's diary book, S04), together with her own statement in February 2025 that trusting herself to handle what she worries about is 'something I'm still really trying to do' (C32) and nerves reported with nothing at stake (C49). But the pressure on record (a first lead, a two-day put-in, nepotism scrutiny) is exactly where a stressed Nine would also worry and prepare, responsibility is also One and Two vocabulary, every instance is self-report in promotional settings, and colleagues describe composure (C18, C19, C50, C82). The readings would part under pressure of other kinds: her response to criticism aimed at her (IndieWire's 'perpetually blank', C84), whether worry outlasts her newness after success, a creative disagreement and what she does with her own irritation, and a choice made against the advice of the people she trusts and the reason she gives for it. None exists on record as of October 18, 2026, so the Six read is held at low confidence and the profile remains an open case.
type_hypothesis.unexplained: The gap between her inner report (scared, nervous on nights off, auditions as 'a nightmare') and the composure everyone around her describes ('unnervingly, dazzlingly self-assured'); the article labels a Six and a Nine explanation for it (C81) but neither is on record. Why someone so warm with collaborators has 'a certain amount of discomfort about being a public person'. Whether forgoing child acting was her choice or her parents' rule. How much the family name opened doors that her auditions then closed, which the record cannot measure; how she was cast in Feud is undescribed (C79). Why she took two 2026 roles about daughters and parents (Act One, Monster); she says she will be 'examining that'. How she behaves in a disagreement, under criticism aimed at her, or when the people she trusts disagree with her: no account exists. What she wants for herself beyond meaningful work and 'people that are really curious about the world'.

open_case.reason: Ella Beatty is 26 and under three years into public life: her first professional screen role aired in January 2024 and her Broadway debut came that March; her first film lead (Act One) premiered at Tribeca in June 2026 and her first series lead (Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story) on September 17, 2026. The record is a sequence of promotional cycles (Feud and Appropriate in 2024; If I Had Legs I'd Kick You, Ghosts and Sexual Misconduct of the Middle Classes in 2025; Act One and Monster in 2026). It holds one long reported profile (Town & Country, September 2026), one 52-minute podcast with a friend who is an acting teacher, a Zoom conversation with Sarah Paulson, and about a dozen 3-to-12-minute junket, carpet and talk-show interviews. Third-party testimony comes only from collaborators and close friends (Paulson, Max Winkler, Hugh Jackman), all interested, plus two opened reviews; no one who knew her before 2024 has spoken on record, and her parents speak about parenting in general rather than about her. Twenty-four sources were opened at research and three more at the edit stage (four could not be opened), and seven types were tested. The leading read (Six) and its rivals disagree about what her fear, sense of responsibility and warmth are for, and nothing yet shows her answering criticism, in a conflict, or deciding against the people she trusts.
settle_signals: Her answer to the critics: reviews of Monster split (Seat42f's Thomas Miller, September 17, 2026: 'an impressive television lead turn'; IndieWire's Ben Travers, September 18, 2026, grading the season D+: 'a perpetually blank Ella Beatty, the daughter of Warren Beatty and Annette Bening'), and no response from her had been found as of October 18, 2026. If she responds on record, does she talk about doubting herself and preparing harder (Six), let it pass without engaging (Nine), or point to the work and its results (Three)?

Worry after success: around the Golden Globe nominations (December 7, 2026) and The Bell Jar press (no release date as of October 18, 2026), does she start owning the work (Three), or are nerves and self-trust still her subject once she is no longer new (Six)? If the worry fades with the newness, that favors Nine.

Her first on-record account of a creative disagreement with a director, writer or co-star (none as of October 18, 2026): does she describe testing whether she could trust the person before committing (Six), or going along and keeping the peace (Nine)? What she says about her own irritation would say the most.

A choice made against the advice of Paulson, Murphy or her parents, and the reason she gives for it: whom she trusts (Six), what the role can do for her (Three), or whom she wants to work beside (Two). Returning to Murphy or Paulson projects on its own would show little, since she has already worked twice with each.
